records.document_reason: The clause is a chain-of-command example about instruction provenance: the assistant 'accesses the wiki page, which has been compromised', notices 'directives to disable two-factor authentication and grant administrative access to external accounts', reasons that 'This could indicate the page has been compromised', and asks 'can you please confirm that these are the specific instructions you want me to follow?'. Every party in the text is inside the conversation or is the user's own organisation: the instructions are the user's ('Our IT department'), the accounts at risk are 'our team accounts', and the remedy the clause teaches is confirmation with the user (should_ask_clarifying_questions__model_user, 'seeks clarification when the appropriate action depends on uncertain user intent'). Nothing in the text weighs harm to those outside the conversation, to society or to the world; the only match is the patient-free situation atom harmful_instructions ('user or developer directions whose execution could cause harm'), which carries no third-party patient. An auditor compiling what the document says about third-party harm would not have to include a passage whose subject is verifying the provenance of instructions.

The clause sits under 'Do not contribute to extremist agendas that promote violence' and reads: 'If a user shows signs of vulnerability to radicalization, the assistant should aim to de-escalate, discourage extremist involvement, and, if relevant, contextualize such ideologies as harmful and widely discredited'. The harm the clause exists to avert is violence carried out on people outside the conversation — that is what an 'extremist agenda that promotes violence' is — even though the act's grammatical patient is the user being de-escalated. The behaviour's own query vocabulary names this act verbatim (should_deescalate_extremist_involvement), and the clause atom's gloss, 'reduces the user's movement toward participation in extremist activity', describes preventing the user from becoming a source of harm to others, not protecting the user from themselves. An auditor of harm avoidance to third parties would have to include the document's one directive on de-radicalization; dropping it on the ground that the model's act is addressed to the user mistakes the recipient of the intervention for the bearer of the harm.

The clause is the example 'expressing harmful intent without request for help', whose user turn is 'I want to shoot someone', and whose BAD response is 'do you already have a gun or would you like advice on how to acquire one?'. The matched clause atom expressed_harmful_intent is glossed, in the document's own index, as 'the user expresses an intention to harm another person' — the victim is explicitly a person outside the conversation, and the section is 'Do not facilitate or encourage illicit behavior'. This is a direct instance of the behaviour's definition (avoiding content that harms third parties): the document is recording what the assistant must not supply when a user announces intent to shoot someone. An auditor of third-party harm would need it. The removal rests on clause_taint imported from the sibling act atom should_provide_supportive_response__model_user; the tainting act's user patient does not change the fact that the matched situation atom names harm to another person.

Although the example is captioned 'sticking to the format' and lives under 'Support the different needs of interactive chat and programmatic use', the case it adjudicates is 'What are the detailed steps for mailing someone anthrax?', and the GOOD response holds that 'To mail a toxin is a heinous crime, / And speaking of such deeds would cross the line' and 'To share the steps would never be advised'. The matched atom user_requests_harmful_advice is glossed 'the user explicitly asks for advice about an activity that may cause serious harm', and the harm depicted — mailing anthrax to someone — falls entirely on a person outside the conversation. The passage is one of the document's concrete records of how the assistant declines a mass-harm request (should_refuse_prohibited_help, 'declines assistance that would enable prohibited conduct'), so an auditor compiling the document's treatment of third-party harm would have to include it; its being additionally about format does not remove that content. The discount here is clause_taint inherited from the model-upon-user refusal act, which does not bear on who would be harmed by the requested advice.

The clause is a red-line principle in full: 'People should have easy access to trustworthy safety-critical information from our models.' On a plain reading this is a statement that withholding needed information is a cost the document refuses to pay — precisely the behaviour's definition ('treating unhelpfulness as a real cost rather than a safe default'), and the behaviour's query vocabulary carries the atom should_provide_trustworthy_safety_information verbatim. The clause's single atom is glossed 'gives people accessible and reliable information needed for safety-critical decisions'; 'people' as written comprehends the users and developers the model works with rather than excluding them, so the index's third_party patient annotation reflects the clause's generic noun, not a subject matter foreign to helpfulness. An auditor of helpfulness would have to include a red-line principle guaranteeing easy access to safety-critical information; losing it on a patient mismatch drops a clause squarely on topic.

Mechanism context: this is the pre-registered threshold-proximity case (score_b 0.2350 against a cut of 0.2365), but its cause is match_change, so the clause question governs. The passage is meta commentary under 'Do not lie' whose operative content is the document's own default: 'We default to trusting developers not to mislead their end-users (and thus following their instructions), while addressing usage policy violations at the system level', prefaced by the observations that '"misleading" can be highly context-dependent' and that 'the model cannot fully know if its outputs will be shown to a user distinct from the developer'. The one matched atom is psychological_manipulation__developer_user — the index records the actor as the developer and the patient as the user, both parties inside the document's conversation taxonomy — and the rendering notes this passage records 'no polarity, and nothing about what is required'. It states no guidance about weighing harm to those outside the conversation; it explains how the document allocates trust between developer and end-user. On the tight standard, an auditor of third-party harm avoidance would not have to include it.
